question: A district health manager wants to compare two malaria control strategies — indoor residual spraying versus insecticide-treated bed nets — by measuring the cost per malaria case prevented. Which health economics tool is MOST appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CBA converts all outcomes, including health outcomes, into monetary terms (e.g., rupees saved from productivity loss). It is used when comparing programmes across sectors with different objectives.

Correct. CEA measures cost per unit of a single, natural health outcome — in this case, cost per malaria case prevented. It is ideal when comparing two interventions for the same health problem using the same outcome metric.

CUA measures cost per QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) or DALY averted. It is used when comparing interventions across different health conditions, not for a single-disease comparison using natural units.
CMA is used only when two interventions have already been proven to have identical outcomes — you then simply compare costs. Here, outcomes are not yet known to be equal, so CEA is appropriate.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is the outcome metric. 'Cost per malaria case prevented' is a natural health unit (not monetary, not utility-weighted) — that points to Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA).
Excellent. CEA is the tool of choice when comparing interventions for the same condition measured in natural health units. Remember: CEA → single outcome; CUA → QALYs/DALYs; CBA → monetary outcomes.
